paras: The lynching of James McHan took place at Pecos, New Mexico Territory, about thirty miles south of Las Vegas, on the night of June 8, 1882, when a mob hanged a young railroad section hand accused of shooting a co-worker. McHan had fled after the killing of John Graves, was captured by about forty men and put under guard, and was then taken from his guards and hanged to a bridge in the station yard. A brief wire report of the case ran in papers from Washington to Nevada in the following two weeks.

McHan and Graves both worked in the track gang on the railroad section at Pecos. According to the special correspondent of the Las Vegas Gazette, the two quarreled "about some trifling affair" the evening before the shooting, and McHan told Graves he would have to take back what he had said or be killed the next morning. The Gazette gave Graves's age as about seventeen and his home as Michigan, and McHan's age as about twenty.

At about six o'clock on the evening of June 8, McHan, armed with a revolver, entered the car where Graves lay on his bunk and challenged him to come outside. As Graves rose, the Gazette said, McHan shot him near the heart, and he died within a few minutes. The wire version described the encounter more briefly as a fight in which McHan killed Graves.

McHan jumped from the car and escaped to the mountains, but about forty men followed, captured him and brought him back, where he was placed under guard. At about eleven o'clock that night a mob took him from the guards and hanged him to the bridge at the east end of the station yard. Both the Gazette and the wire reported the next day that the body was still hanging.
No report of an inquest, of arrests or of any official response appears in the coverage.

The only local account was the Gazette's special from Pecos, which called the shooting "A cold Hooded [blooded] murder" and headlined that McHan "Pajs the Penalty at a Ropes End." Elsewhere the story came from the Denver Republican's Las Vegas correspondent and ran on June 10 in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, the National Republican and the Salt Lake Herald, the last under the headline "Summary Justice-Captured." The Sacramento Daily Record-Union carried the same Las Vegas dispatch that day under "Murderers Captured—One Lynch[ed]."

Weekly papers then condensed the item into news summaries, among them the Silver State in Nevada, the Watertown Republican and Kenosha Telegraph in Wisconsin, the Iowa Plain Dealer, the Iola Register and the Bismarck Tribune. Mississippi and Ohio papers printed the name as "McHare," and the Bismarck Tribune as "McHair." None of the reports gave the race of either man, and none commented on the mob's action.

The wire said McHan was from East Saginaw, Michigan, while the local Gazette said his home was not known and that he was "said to bo a wandering tramp," giving Michigan instead as Graves's home. The Gazette's on-the-spot account is also fuller on the shooting, which it described as a deliberate attack on a reclining man rather than the "fight" or "affray" of the wire and weekly versions.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob took McHan from his guards and hanged him to a bridge after he was accused of killing a fellow section hand (A1, A2, A11).

McHan was hanged by a mob, without any legal process reported, after a party of about forty men captured him for the killing of John Graves (A1, A2, A11). No paper gives his race, so whether the case is anti-Black violence is unknown.

The local Las Vegas Gazette special (A1) and the Denver Republican's Las Vegas wire (A2, A6), which differ on the victim's origin and so appear independent, agree on the killing of Graves, the capture by about forty men and the lynching.
